Marco Polo was a thirteenth-century Venetian merchant and explorer whose account of his journey to the court of Kublai Khan opened European awareness of Asia. He left Venice in 1271 as a young teenager and traveled overland to China with his father and uncle, taking over three years to reach Kublai Khan's court. The Mongol ruler granted him the title of Messere—Mister—and employed him directly, possibly as a diplomat and administrator.

During his time in Asia, he traveled extensively throughout the Mongol Empire, visiting regions of modern-day China, Burma, and Southeast Asia, gathering geographical and political intelligence. He returned to Venice in 1295 after twenty-four years away, bringing jewels and letters of recommendation from Kublai Khan. While imprisoned after a naval battle, he dictated his memoirs to a fellow prisoner, Rustichello of Pisa. These writings became The Travels of Marco Polo, also called Il Milione.

His account described the wealth, culture, and organization of the Yuan Dynasty in terms that shocked Europeans—tales of vast cities, paper money, and advanced governance unlike anything in Western Europe. His book spread knowledge of Asia throughout Europe, though some scholars note inconsistencies in his account and question whether he traveled the full route or relied partly on hearsay. Nonetheless, later explorers like Christopher Columbus were inspired partly by reading accounts like Marco Polo's, seeking their own western route to reach the riches of Asia.
